https://yubanet.com/regional/the-invinci.text: Come celebrate an early Silent Movie Day with the Invincible Czars, the acclaimed silent film soundtrack ensemble, accompanying Robert Wiene’s highly stylized 1920 German horror film The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari at The Onyx Downtown at the Nevada Theatre, 401 Broad Street, Nevada City. Remarkable in many ways, the film’s disorienting sets, heavy makeup, and overall treatment make it the classic example of German Expressionism. It was also made in a rare open window: film censorship in Germany had been abolished in November 1918 and would not be reinstated until May 1920, so Caligari was written, shot, and released during the only period in German history when filmmakers faced no state restrictions. Screenwriters Carl Mayer (Austrian) and Hans Janowitz (born in Prague) used that freedom for a deliberate attack on authority — the state as hypnotist, the citizen as a sleepwalker made to kill. Filming took place in the winter of 1919–20, in the first months of the Weimar Republic, the democratic German state that would stand until Hitler’s rise in 1933. The film’s innovations include one of the earliest known examples of situational typography interacting with a scene through visual effects — hand-lettered words erupting across the landscape via stop-motion animation — and an early, enormously influential instance of staging violence as shadow, the compositional template horror still uses. (Remember the shower scene in Psycho ?) Be the first to know, sign up for our newsletter, absolutely free of course. Audiences may remember The Invincible Czars from their 2025 Onyx Downtown screening of Phantom of the Opera, which played to a full house. Their return promises another unforgettable night where silent film, dramatic enactment, and live music combine for an experience unlike any other. As with Phantom , the ensemble will feature a Foley artist providing a wide range of live sound effects. Formed in Austin, Texas, The Invincible Czars have been reinventing the silent film experience since 2003. This is their third performance at the Nevada Theatre. The band notes that Caligari ‘s craggy edges, disjointed backgrounds, and heavy makeup have inspired filmmakers such as Tim Burton and musician David Bowie, and that its twist ending is widely considered the first in cinematic history — a device Rod Serling’s The Twilight Zone would later make its own. “We strive to create soundtracks that give modern-day audiences a context to appreciate these 100-year-old movies,” said Josh Robins, Invincible Czars founder and bandleader. The band encourages attendees to dress for the Halloween season — even when it isn’t Halloween season. Audiences in Nevada City will have a rare opportunity to experience one of the earliest horror films, with its astonishing sets and still-timely social commentary, in a way that bridges past and present: on the big screen, in the Nevada Theatre, built in 1865, accompanied by a modern live score and inventive live Foley throughout. Tickets are available now and are expected to sell quickly for this early Silent Movie Day celebration. The film is co-presented by The Onyx Theatre and the Nevada City Film Festival. https://www.politico.eu/article/brussels.text: LONDON — The European Union has just offered Canada “associate EU membership.” Don’t expect it to do the same for Brexit Britain. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen’s surprise announcement came during her State of the Union address in Strasbourg on Wednesday. “We share one ocean, one set of values, one way of seeing the world,” she said, inviting Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney to help make his country “the first associate member of the European Union.” Advertisement Advertisement Could Britain be the second? The idea of “associate membership” has already piqued the interest of some in London. Ten years after voters chose to leave the EU, lawmakers in Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s ruling Labour Party are looking for ways to unpick the Brexit settlement without re-opening old political wounds. “We need to be as close to the EU as possible, in the hopes we can find a way back in,” said Bell Ribeiro-Addy, a Labour MP who once rebelled to vote against former Prime Minister Boris Johnson’s Brexit deal. “If an associate arrangement gets us closer, even as a stepping stone, Britain should be asking for it — not watching from the sidelines.” Another Labour MP, Clive Lewis, told POLITICO: “Anything that can drag us away from the Starmer government’s disastrous hyper-Atlanticism and closer to the EU has to be considered.” A “natural question” Diplomats from EU member countries sympathetic to closer cooperation with the U.K. are also pondering whether the status is a good fit. Advertisement Advertisement “It is a natural question,” one EU envoy told POLITICO as to whether the U.K. might be able seek a similar deal. The envoy, who like others quoted in this story was granted anonymity to speak about the sensitive topic, added: “We have several similar partners that would be interested and we will have to see what it means in practice.” But decision-makers in Brussels have been quick to nip the idea in the bud. One senior EU official told POLITICO that von der Leyen’s offer to Canada is about cutting a deal for a country normally ineligible to join the EU. It isn’t for European countries with commitment issues. “Unlike Ukraine, Moldova, Georgia, Norway and the U.K., Canada is not in Europe,” the senior EU official said. “It cannot join the EU. Norway shouldn’t be looking at this and thinking ‘oh we want more.’ This isn’t for them. Their route to that is to join the EU. Same for the U.K.” Advertisement Advertisement Just as well then that the British government is not currently exploring the idea, according to one person familiar with U.K. government thinking on EU policy. Instead, Burnham’s government is focused on wrapping up a “reset” of relations by his predecessor Keir Starmer. This relatively modest program includes a deal to smooth trade in agri-food, establish a youth mobility scheme, and sign an agreement to coordinate emissions trading. The deals are meant to be signed off at an EU-U.K. summit to be held by the end of the year. The meeting is yet to be scheduled, however, and talks have been complicated by disputes over EU protectionism on steel and procurement, as well as wrangling over the rate of tuition fees paid by European students studying in Britain. You say associate, I say ally It’s unclear whether von der Leyen’s proposal will go anywhere. Carney hasn’t actually asked to become a member of anything — rather, he told delegates Tuesday at an investment summit in Toronto that he wanted to build a “unique security and economic alliance” with Europe. Reports ahead of Carney’s speech that he would be proposing associate EU membership appear not to have come true — though von der Leyen seemed to respond on Wednesday as if they had. Yet practically, Canada and the EU are not even using their existing cooperation to full effect. Ten EU member countries including France, Poland and Italy are yet to ratify the EU-Canada free trade agreement, CETA, nearly a decade after it was signed. Advertisement Advertisement Even so, there may be lessons for the U.K. in the EU’s response to Canada’s approach. “Even if this doesn’t progress past aspiration there can be no doubting that Mark Carney has shown what you can achieve with a clear ambitious message, and a focus on common challenges not red lines,” Stella Creasy, the MP who chairs the Labour Movement for Europe, told POLITICO. “For the UK, it’s a sobering reminder that if we don’t rebuild our partnerships for peace and prosperity with our neighbors, others will.” Gabriel Gavin reported from Brussels
